paper.title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
paper.abstract: Comprehensively characterizing cellular diversity is critical for understanding tissue development, identifying disease-associated populations and investigating gene programmes linked to specialized functions. Advances in single-cell profiling reveal additional cell-specific transcripts and molecular associations, yet many foundation models represent only a restricted portion of this increasingly rich molecular information. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression in a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million cell profiles spanning 40 species, CellNet improves rare-population and condition-associated state recognition in evaluated cohorts while retaining competitive general cell representations. It predicts withheld coding-gene expression and selected non-coding targets in total-RNA data, and recovers lineage-specific expression patterns in spatial measurements. Prediction also extends across species, including to targets without expression-pretraining exposure. Its gene representations retrieve known non-coding modules and developmental or neural programmes, including from sparsely detected RNA queries. Together, these results establish CellNet as a scalable framework for interpreting cellular diversity through increasingly comprehensive transcriptomic measurements.

also.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
also.abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

also.title: What comes after de novo? Automated lead optimization of proteins with CRADLE-1
also.abstract: Lead optimization remains the longest and most expensive step in pre-clinical drug discovery, typically consuming 12-36 months whilst costing $5M-$15M per candidate. We introduce 'CRADLE-1', an automated framework for protein engineering. While CRADLE-1 supports the full process of drug discovery and industrial protein engineering pipelines, including hit identification and de novo binder design, this work focuses on its application to multi-property lead optimization across protein modalities (VHHs, scFvs, IgGs, peptides, enzymes, CRISPR systems, vaccines). We show it is 4-7x faster than rational design, as measured by the number of wet lab rounds required. We provide in-vitro validation across all of the above modalities, typically optimizing multiple properties simultaneously (single and polyspecific binding down to picomolar, activity, thermostability, ...). Technically, CRADLE-1 starts with pre-trained foundation protein language models (PLMs), which are fine-tuned in unsupervised fashion on evolutionary neighborhoods, in supervised fashion using lab-in-the-loop data, and then deployed in a multi-model workflow. Of additional interest, we find that (a) the end-to-end system may be run in automated fashion; (b) wet lab data may be consumed in 'black box' fashion without knowledge of the underlying biochemical mechanisms; (c) structural data may largely be superseded by sequence-function pairs.

also.title: AutoOnboarder: Autonomously Onboarding LLM Agents
also.abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.
